title: Before ICE: three American mass removals, what they killed, and what the public said at the time
dek: The 1930s repatriations, the wartime camps and Operation Wetback. One had a death count and a 93 percent approval rating; one had 88 dead in an afternoon and a president at 75 percent; one was never counted or polled at all. What the record says about judging the fourth.
body:
The United States has run a mass removal or mass detention program three times before this one: the Mexican “repatriations” of the Depression, the wartime incarceration of Japanese Americans, and the 1954 campaign the government itself named Operation Wetback. For each, historians can now say roughly how many people were taken and, for two of the three, how many died. For two of the three there is also a record of what the public thought at the time. Set beside the present program, the three episodes answer the question a reader put to The Watch this week, how the deaths compare with the approval, in a way the current numbers alone cannot: approval at the time has been almost no guide to how the country judged the episode later, and the deaths were rarely counted until it was over.

## 1929 to 1936: a million, or half a million, and no one counting

The first mass removal was not, mostly, a deportation. The Department of Homeland Security’s own historical table shows the formal removals of those years running between 13,877 and 31,035 a year, numbers smaller than a slow month today [1]. The rest of the departures were produced by raids, by welfare offices that offered a one-way train ticket as the alternative to losing relief, and by fear [2][3]. How many left is contested across a factor of four. Abraham Hoffman’s 1974 study put it at 400,000 to 500,000 between 1929 and 1937, with a peak of 138,000 in 1931, and a 2021 economic study by Jongkwan Lee, Giovanni Peri and Vasil Yasenov called the lower figure the better documented one [2]. Francisco Balderrama and Raymond Rodríguez, whose book “Decade of Betrayal” brought the episode back into public view, put it at more than a million and called that conservative [3]. The California state senator who carried the apology bill in 2005, Joe Dunn, used 1.8 million [4].

What the historians agree on is who was removed. Balderrama estimates that at least 60 percent were United States citizens, most of them children born here to Mexican parents [3]. Lee, Peri and Yasenov, using census records, put the U.S.-born share at a quarter to a third [2]. Either way, this was the removal of hundreds of thousands of Americans.

Nobody counted the dead. No study The Watch could find, academic or journalistic, gives a death toll for the repatriations, and the agent of removal in most cases was a county welfare office rather than a federal one, so there was no custody in which to die and no agency obliged to report it [2][3]. Nor was there polling: George Gallup began his national surveys in 1935, as the removals were ending, and no survey about the removals is known; Gallup’s earliest surviving question on illegal immigration dates from 1977 [5].

The judgment came 70 years later. In 2005 California passed the Apology Act for the 1930s Mexican Repatriation Program, acknowledging “the fundamental violations” of civil liberties and due process; Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger signed it on October 7, 2005, and vetoed the companion bill that would have created a reparations commission [6][29]. No federal apology has followed.

## 1942 to 1946: 120,313 held, 1,862 dead, 93 percent approval

The one program for which both numbers exist from the start is the incarceration of Japanese Americans. The War Relocation Authority’s final statistical report counted 120,313 people in its custody over the life of the camps, 5,981 births and 1,862 deaths [7]. The federal commission that reviewed the episode in 1982, in “Personal Justice Denied,” reproduced the figures and noted that the WRA had claimed death rates in the camps lower than in the general population; it also recorded the day in December 1942 when military police at Manzanar fired on a crowd, killing two and wounding nine [8].

The approval was measured as it happened. In March and April 1942 the National Opinion Research Center asked whether the government had done the right thing in moving Japanese aliens away from the Pacific coast: 93 percent said yes, 1 percent no. Asked about American citizens of Japanese ancestry, 59 percent favored removing them too, 25 percent opposed [9]. (The poll is often credited to Gallup; it was NORC’s.) Gallup’s own question came in December 1942: should the people in the camps be allowed to return to the coast after the war? Thirty-five percent said yes, 48 percent no, and of those who said no, half said they should be sent to Japan [10].

Here the ratio a reader might compute is a trap worth walking into on purpose. Eighteen hundred and sixty-two deaths among about 110,000 people over roughly three and a half years is a death rate near 480 per 100,000 a year, eight or nine times this year’s rate in ICE detention [7][11]. It is also, as the WRA pointed out, below the death rate of the American population at the time, because the camps held entire communities, infants to the very old, while ICE holds working-age adults [8]. The number that is not in dispute is the first one: 120,313 people, two-thirds of them citizens, held for years on the strength of a 93 percent poll [7][27][9].

The judgment took 46 years. The Civil Liberties Act of 1988, signed by Ronald Reagan on August 10 of that year, apologized on behalf of the nation and paid $20,000 to each surviving internee; 82,219 people received the payment, the first checks going out in October 1990 [12].

## 1954: a million claimed, 300,000 likely, 88 dead in an afternoon

Operation Wetback began on June 9, 1954, under a new immigration commissioner, retired Gen. Joseph Swing, with the Border Patrol sweeping first the Southwest and then the cities [13][14]. The government’s number for the year was spectacular. The Immigration and Naturalization Service reported 1,035,282 apprehensions in the fiscal year that ended three weeks after the operation began, and the Department of Homeland Security’s historical table still records 1,074,277 “returns” for fiscal 1954, against 232,769 the next year [13][1]. Swing claimed to have “hurled more than one million Mexicans deep into Mexico” [13].

Historians do not believe him. Kelly Lytle Hernández of UCLA, whose history of the Border Patrol is the standard account, puts the campaign’s own removals at fewer than 300,000; the million was a fiscal-year total padded with routine border turn-backs and with people the government assumed had left on their own [13][14]. Britannica’s entry gives the same range [15].

What the campaign did to the people it caught is better documented than how many there were. To prevent them from walking back, the government carried deportees deep into Mexico: by bus to staging areas, by train to the interior, and by ship, the Emancipación and the Mercurio, from Port Isabel, Texas, to Veracruz [16]. In the summer of 1955, after a roundup in 112-degree heat, 88 men died of sunstroke before the Red Cross intervened, by the account of the Columbia historian Mae Ngai [17][18]. On one Gulf voyage, a riot aboard an overcrowded ship ended with deportees drowning; Ngai’s count is five, other accounts say seven [19][18]. In August 1956, with about 500 people aboard the Mercurio and two lifeboats rated for 96, 32 men jumped overboard near Tampico in protest; the Associated Press dispatch reported no deaths [20]. A congressional inquiry described conditions on the ship as those of an “18th-century slave ship,” and the ship deportations ended [13][17].

The approval was measured, but not of the program. Gallup, in the series compiled by the American Presidency Project, had Dwight Eisenhower at 62 percent the week the operation began, 75 percent a month later, 57 percent that November, and between 66 and 78 percent through 1955 [21][22]. Nobody asked the public about the roundups; Gallup’s earliest surviving question on illegal immigration is from 1977 [5]. So the only ratio available is the president’s: a leader near the height of his popularity, running a campaign that killed 88 people in a day, which the public did not rate because it was not asked.

The judgment here was quicker and quieter: the congressional investigation within two years, then decades in which the operation was remembered mainly by the people it touched, until it returned to national politics in 2015 as a model one presidential candidate said he would follow [17][14].

## What the three episodes say about the fourth

Set the present program in the sequence and three things stand out.

First, the counting. Of the four programs, only the current one has produced a running public tally of its dead while it was under way: ICE’s death-reporting page, with all its delays, and the researchers who check it [11]. The repatriations produced none. The camps produced an exact count, but only in a report issued after they closed [7]. Operation Wetback’s 88 survive in a historian’s footnote [17]. The 36 deaths in ICE custody in fiscal 2026 are the first deaths of an American mass-enforcement program to be known to the public, in rough real time, as a number [28].

Second, the approval. The only earlier program measured while it ran had 93 percent behind it, and that approval turned out to be worth nothing to its reputation 46 years on [9][12]. The present program has had, in poll after poll this year, majorities saying its enforcement has gone too far [24][25]. There is no earlier case of a mass-enforcement program losing the public while it was still running. In the historical record, the public has either approved or not been asked.

Third, the ratio the reader asked for does exist, in the only form the record supports. Deaths per person held, per year: about 480 per 100,000 in the camps, for a whole population; perhaps 55 in ICE detention this year, for working-age adults screened at intake; unknown for the other two [7][11]. Approval while the program ran: 93 percent, unknown, unknown, and about 38 percent [9][21][26]. The present program is at once the least approved and the best counted of the four, and the first in which the public has had the deaths in front of it while deciding. Whether that changes the judgment that comes later is the one number no one can compute yet.
